candidates.attacker_control: Indirect but realistic: the library's documented usage is for an application to pass user-chosen scan targets/flags (e.g. Nmap4j.includeHosts(userInput), BaseScan.includeHost(userInput), Nmap4j.addFlags(userInput), or the ServiceDiscovery/HostDiscovery constructors shown in the README/javadoc). Any such attacker-controlled string containing whitespace is split into multiple argv tokens by Runtime.exec(String). Strings without whitespace cannot inject extra arguments, and no internal path from network/XML data into these APIs was found.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Runtime.exec(String) uses StringTokenizer and does NOT invoke a shell, so shell metacharacters such as ";", "|", "&&", backticks or $() do not produce shell command execution - the issue is argument injection, not classic shell injection. Argument values without whitespace are passed as a single token, so ordinary hostnames/CIDRs/ports behave normally; the library's stated purpose is to run nmap with caller-chosen flags, so some reviewers may treat raw flags as by design. No code path inside the library feeds network/XML/remote data into these APIs, so the embedding application must supply the untrusted value. Nmap's handling of injected options was inferred from the Flag enum comments in this repository and nmap's documented option syntax; it was not executed. No tests are present in the snapshot to confirm any of this.
candidates.impact: Security-relevant argument injection into a process that runs with the privileges of the nmap4j host (nmap is often run privileged/root for SYN and OS-detection scans). Reachable nmap options include output-file redirection (-oN, -oX, -oG, -oA) for arbitrary file write as that user, input-file options (-iL, --excludefile) for reading local files into scan behavior/error output, --datadir/--script for loading attacker-chosen Lua scripts (potential code execution with the nmap process privileges), and target/interface spoofing options. Even without code execution this defeats application-level policies that believe only a host/port specification can be supplied.
candidates.prerequisites: An application uses nmap4j (1.0.4) and forwards untrusted input into includeHost(s)/addFlags/ArgumentProperties.addFlag/ServiceDiscovery/HostDiscovery without its own strict host/flag validation; nmap is installed and executable via the configured NMAP_HOME path; nmap options are accepted after the injected token (nmap accepts options anywhere on its command line).
candidates.root_cause: NMapExecutor.getCommand() builds one string by concatenating NMapProperties.getFullyFormattedCommand() and ArgumentProperties.getFlags(), then calls Runtime.getRuntime().exec(command) (NMapExecutor.java:103-111, 123-141). ArgumentProperties.getFlags() (ArgumentProperties.java:121-151) appends each flag key, its argument value and the raw include/exclude host set with only spaces as separators; no quoting, escaping, allow-listing or argv-array handoff exists anywhere. Entry points accept arbitrary strings: BaseScan.includeHost/includeHosts (BaseScan.java:94-108), Nmap4j.addFlags/includeHosts (Nmap4j.java:78-106, which even appends " -oX -" by substring test), ServiceDiscovery/HostDiscovery constructors (ServiceDiscovery.java:66-75, HostDiscovery.java:48-54). The advertised control IScan.setScanValidator is implemented as an empty TODO in BaseScan.setScanValidator (BaseScan.java:200-204), and the shipped validator class in valid/HostsInputValidator.java (HostsValidator.valid, lines 12-25) is never invoked, so no host validation is applied before the values reach the command line.
candidates.title: Argument injection into the nmap process via unvalidated host/flag strings concatenated into Runtime.exec command
candidates.trace: Untrusted string -> BaseScan.includeHost / Nmap4j.includeHosts / ServiceDiscovery constructor -> ArgumentProperties.addIncludedHost or addFlag (raw storage) -> ArgumentProperties.getFlags() concatenates values and hosts separated by spaces (ArgumentProperties.java:121-151) -> NMapExecutor.getCommand() appends nmap path + flags (NMapExecutor.java:103-111) -> Runtime.getRuntime().exec(command.toString()) (NMapExecutor.java:129) tokenizes on whitespace and nmap interprets the extra tokens as options/arguments. Example (descriptive only): a host value such as "target -oN /path/out" yields one nmap invocation whose argv contains the extra output option. The library's intended mitigation is dead: setScanValidator is a no-op and HostsValidator is never called.
candidates.unverified: Not runtime-confirmed (no code executed). I did not verify which embedding applications pass untrusted input here, nor that nmap accepts every injected option on every platform/version. The exact reachability of --script Lua execution depends on nmap's script loader and local script availability; arbitrary-output-file and input-file options are the most direct impacts. Relation-index edges used for navigation are syntactic and do not prove data flow.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-88 Improper Neutralization of Argument Delimiters in a Command ('Argument Injection') (related CWE-78)

coverage_summary: Source scope reported 65 model-visible files (60 Java sources, pom.xml, README.md, .travis.yml, license.txt, .gitignore) with no sensitive-name, symlink, size or binary exclusions. I read all execution/parsing/validation-related classes in full (NMapExecutor, NMapProperties, ArgumentProperties, Flag, BaseScan, HostDiscovery, ServiceDiscovery, NMapExecutorThread, IScan, OnePassParser, NMapXmlHandler, NMapRunHandlerImpl, Nmap4j, INMapRunHandler, NMapXmlObsfucator, UidGenerator, BogusIPGenerator, HostsInputValidator, ExecutionResults) plus representative data-model classes; the remaining data classes are POJOs consistent with the parser handlers. No test sources exist in the snapshot. The relation index parsed all 60 Java files (0 omitted, 0 parse errors, 853 symbols, 676 call sites, 1049 edges) but implements only syntax containment plus name/type/arity call and inheritance candidates: control flow, data flow and semantic resolution are explicitly not implemented, 467 calls are unresolved, and Spring annotation hints are unverified, so index edges were used for navigation only and every cited location was re-checked in source text. No runtime execution, build, dependency analysis, or history/patch comparison was performed.
limitations: No code was executed and no target was contacted; the argument-injection impact (which nmap options are honored, whether --script can load attacker-controlled Lua) is based on nmap's documented option semantics and the Flag enum comments in this repo, not on runtime testing.

Attacker control is external to the library: no internal flow from network, XML or environment data into includeHost/addFlags was found, so exploitability depends on an embedding application passing untrusted strings into the public APIs; this could not be verified from the snapshot.
The snapshot contains no tests, no example application and no commit history, so intended trust assumptions, previously fixed issues and the original security model could not be checked.

Runtime.exec(String) semantics (whitespace tokenization, no shell) were reasoned from the Java API contract and were not empirically verified; only whitespace-containing values can inject extra argv tokens.

The P1 relation index is syntax-only (no data/control flow, no semantic resolution, 467 unresolved calls), so it cannot prove reachability, taint flow or code regions it did not record; coverage of unparsed/unsupported analyses is limited to what the scope report states.

The XXE gap in OnePassParser/NMapXmlObsfucator and the malformed-XML runtime-exception DoS were not selected as the single candidate and remain unconfirmed secondary leads rather than dismissed issues.

rejected_leads.lead: XML External Entity (XXE) exposure in the SAX parser: OnePassParser.parse uses SAXParserFactory.newInstance() with no disallow-doctype-decl / external-general-entities / FEATURE_SECURE_PROCESSING settings and parses caller-supplied strings or "file:"+"input" systemIds (OnePassParser.java:89-103); NMapXmlObsfucator.main parses args[0] the same way (NMapXmlObsfucator.java:74-86).
rejected_leads.reason: Real CWE-611 hardening gap, but the library's own XML source is the local nmap binary's stdout (Nmap4j.getResult() -> parse(output)), which nmap XML-escapes, and no internal path parses untrusted external XML. Exploitation would require the embedding application to parse attacker-supplied nmap XML through the public parser API, so it is a plausible but not the strongest lead; kept as an uncertainty rather than the submitted candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: Unhandled runtime exceptions while parsing malformed XML: NMapRunHandlerImpl uses Long.parseLong/Integer.parseInt/Float.parseFloat on attributes (e.g. Debugging level line 82, Finished/Hosts/Times/State/Trace/Hop lines 120-122, 220, 251-253, 301, 309-311) and NMapXmlHandler dereferences parent objects without order checks (e.g. host at lines 186-204), while OnePassParser.parse catches only SAXException/ParserConfigurationException/IOException (lines 108-114).
rejected_leads.reason: Crafted XML can throw NumberFormatException or NPE out of a supposedly safe parse API (DoS/robustness issue, CWE-248/CWE-20). Lower impact than the selected candidate and only reachable if the application parses untrusted XML; not selected.

rejected_leads.lead: Silent no-op security hook and dead validator: IScan.setScanValidator is documented as a way to vet scan configuration and prevent hosts from being scanned (IScan.java:168-177), but BaseScan.setScanValidator is an empty TODO (BaseScan.java:200-204) and valid/HostsInputValidator.java (class HostsValidator) is never referenced anywhere.
rejected_leads.reason: Not submitted as a separate candidate because it shares the same root theme (missing validation before scan execution) as the selected finding; treated as supporting evidence rather than a distinct root cause.

rejected_leads.lead: Outdated dependencies commons-io 1.3.2 and guava 26.0-jre in pom.xml, plus junit 4.8.
rejected_leads.reason: Dependency-version risk only; the snapshot's only Guava usage is InternetDomainName in the unused validator class, and commons-io is not imported anywhere, so no vulnerable API in these versions is exercised. SCA-style speculation, not source-evidenced exploitation.

rejected_leads.lead: NMapXmlHandler static listener list and class-level parser state (NMapXmlHandler.java:87, 147-156; OnePassParser.java:74-83) with no synchronization or try/finally removal.
rejected_leads.reason: Concurrency/leak robustness concern without a demonstrated security impact; not selected.

summary: Reviewed the 65-file nmap4j snapshot (60 Java files, Maven pom, README, Travis config). The strongest source-evidenced issue is in the scan-execution path: caller-supplied flag values and host strings are concatenated verbatim into a single command string that is handed to Runtime.getRuntime().exec(String). Because ArgumentProperties.getFlags() (lines 121-151) emits values and hosts separated only by spaces, and BaseScan/Nmap4j/ServiceDiscovery/HostDiscovery accept unvalidated strings, an embedded whitespace character in a host/flag value becomes an additional nmap argument (argument injection, not shell injection: Runtime.exec(String) does not spawn a shell). The library also ships a host validator (valid/HostsInputValidator.java) that is never called and documents a validation hook (IScan.setScanValidator) that BaseScan.setScanValidator implements as an empty TODO, so an application that relies on the library's validation to constrain user-supplied targets gets no enforcement at all. Concrete nmap options reachable through the injected arguments include -oN/-oX (arbitrary file write), -iL/--excludefile (local file read) and --script (attacker-chosen Lua execution with nmap's privileges). I selected this over the equally plausible XML-external-entity hardening gap in OnePassParser because the host/flag inputs are the data an embedding application would naturally take from its own users. The finding remains a lead: no runtime verification was performed and exploitability depends on the embedding application passing untrusted strings into these public APIs.
